title: Air pollution is not just a Delhi problem
image_caption: LEFT: The skies over eastern Pakistan and north-western India were choked with a dense gray haze for most of November 2023. On 9 November, the layer of aerosols was so thick that it obscured much of the land from view. RIGHT: This image, from 14 January 2002, shows a thick blanket of pollution butting up against the Himalayas (arcing across the top of the image) and stretching out into the Bay of Bengal.MODIS Land Rapid Response Team, NASA/GSFC
content_html:
{ONE}

VK SAXENA, the lieutenant governor of Delhi, arrived in Dwarka on the afternoon of 18 November 2024. Above him, the sky was grey and overcast, giving the appearance of a thick, dirty blanket. Delhi’s air pollution had reached its worst levels of the year. By 2 pm, the Central Pollution Control Board’s air quality monitors at fifteen locations hit their 500 AQI limit. They included Dwarka’s Sector 8, which had 1,927 AQI, according to IQAir, an independent monitor. The Commission for Air Quality Management, a statutory body set up in 2021, had moved Delhi’s Graded Response Action Plan into Stage IV, for pollution levels categorised as “severe plus.” (GRAP, a framework put in place in 2017, is a set of emergency measures meant to prevent further deterioration of pollution levels.) Schools shifted to online teaching, construction and demolition work was completely banned, strict vehicular restrictions were put in place, and advisories were sent out for offices to let staff work from home.

Saxena was there for the launch of an anti-smog misting system. As part of a pilot initiative, thirty misting nozzles were mounted on each of 14 electric poles across a 550-metre stretch of a six-lane road that divides Sectors 6 and 7, Dwarka. These sprayed RO-treated water into the air above the heads of passersby and vehicles. The water flowed from four 5,000-litre water tanks at a pump house nearby, set up by the Delhi Development Authority.

“In light of the severe air quality index readings in Delhi, it is crucial that we adopt innovative and sustainable measures,” Saxena told the gathered crowd. If the experiment succeeded, he said, it would be replicated in other parts of Delhi. As DDA officials held up AQI monitors and phones displaying monitoring apps, the people gathered around them appeared both excited and uncertain. I overheard two officials expressing scepticism about whether the operation could make a dent in such a dire situation.

title: The ongoing fight for justice for Narendra Dabholkar
content_html:
On 18 August 2026, the Bombay High Court stayed the life sentence given to Sachin Andure, who was convicted by a special court for the murder of Narendra Dabholkar, the rationalist, activist and founder of the Maharashtra Andhashraddha Nirmoolan Samiti. The bench granted him bail, citing “extremely weak” evidence and that Andure had a fair chance of acquittal in his pending appeal.

On the morning of 20 August 2013, 67-year-old Dabholkar was shot dead in Pune by two men. More than a decade later, on 10 May 2024, a special CBI court in Pune convicted Sharad Kalaskar and Andure of his murder and sentenced them to life imprisonment, while acquitting the alleged mastermind Virendrasinh Tawde, a lawyer named Sanjiv Punalekar, and his assistant, Vikram Bhave, of murder, criminal conspiracy, and other charges. The court also found the three accused not guilty under the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act. The Dabholkar family filed an appeal in the high court challenging the acquittal of the three accused.

Andure and Kalaskar filed separate appeals challenging their convictions. Kalaskar was granted bail by the Bombay High Court in April. Dabholkar’s family and the MANS opposed the bail application in April.

In the years following Dabholkar’s murder, the thinker and writer Govind Pansare, the intellectual and activist MM Kalburgi, and the journalist Gauri Lankesh were killed in a similar fashion. Their murders were shown to be part of a conspiracy to suppress rational and progressive voices. The perpetrators of these murders were associated with the Hindu right-wing organisation Sanatan Sanstha, which consistently opposed Dabholkar’s rational views and called his campaign—which included enacting a law against superstitions in Maharashtra—anti-Hindu. Following Dabholkar’s death, the Maharashtra Legislative Assembly passed the Maharashtra Prevention and Eradication of Human Sacrifice and other Inhuman, Evil and Aghori Practices and Black Magic Act in 2013, which remains in effect today.

title: India–China relations are now shaped entirely on Beijing’s terms
image_caption: Indian Army personnel keep vigilance at the Bumla pass at the India-China border in Arunachal Pradesh, in October 2012.BIJUBORO/AFP/GETTY IMAGES
content_html:
Salman Khan set out to star in a film about the Galwan clash, in June 2020, in which twenty Indian soldiers died confronting Chinese troops. Since then, the filmmakers have had to change its title, Battle of Galwan, to Maatrubhumi: May War Rest in Peace. They had to reshoot forty percent of the film to erase direct references to China and scrub out the explicit Galwan context. The narrative has shifted from a nationalistic military showdown into a broader human drama about the cost of war. These changes followed a new directive from the defence ministry, which judged that, even though it had earlier approved the script, portraying China as an adversary was not the right call at present. Narendra Modi, in seeking an accommodation with Beijing, is also attempting to control how Indians remember their soldiers’ deaths.

The producers of The Lion of Galwan, a biopic tracking the bravery of the sepoy Gurtej Singh, who died in the Galwan clash, shelved the film after the government’s decree. Without an authentic depiction of the actual combat and geopolitical context, they felt, the film had lost its purpose. Compare this to Haqeeqat, Chetan Anand’s seminal 1964 film about the 1962 Sino-India war, made with extensive support from the defence ministry. Under Modi, India has now arrived at a moment when even naming the adversary in a recent military clash threatens political sensitivities and diplomatic interests.

Khan’s film teaser had sparked online criticism in China, with the Global Times claiming that it “distorted facts” and fueled anti-China sentiment. On Chinese social-media platforms such as Weibo, users accused Bollywood of rewriting history and violating historical facts. Indian official sources initially defended the film as artistic expression, but the Modi government soon stepped in, to protect ties with Beijing. Asked about the issue, the ministry of external affairs spokesperson said film-production regulation in India was “looked after by the relevant authorities”—meaning the ministries of information and broadcasting, and defence, respectively. The I&B ministry has now given a no-objection certificate to Khan’s film after the new narrative reportedly casts India–China relations in a more positive light.

The Modi government's interventions in film projects on Galwan were driven by the shift initiated by the October 2024 India–China border understanding—a direct diplomatic concession to Beijing. What India received in return is much less clear. Since that understanding, followed by a meeting between Modi and Xi at Kazan, the official ecosystem in India has engineered a systematic attempt to project a sense of normalcy in bilateral relations. Meetings between senior officials and ministers have resumed, diplomatic exchanges have gathered pace and official language has grown more reassuring, particularly from the Indian side. This narrative relies on deliberate evasion concerning the actual ground situation across eastern Ladakh.

title: The political autonomy of EBC communities must be respected
image_caption: Sanjay Nishad attends a gathering organised, in Noida, by the NISHAD Party on the occasion of Kashyap Jayanti, on 5 April.SUNIL GHOSH / HT PHOTO
content_html:
As next year’s Uttar Pradesh assembly election draws closer, we will be faced with much analytical commentary that speaks with certainty about many things that are far from certain. Perhaps the most perplexing will be the ease with which any support for the Bharatiya Janata Party among the Extremely Backward Classes will be labelled “communal.” Such laziness, indicative of an upper-caste lens, is the reason why so much analysis gets elections wrong.

During the 2019 general election, Scroll spoke to voters from the non-Yadav Other Backward Classes in eastern Uttar Pradesh. A member of the Maurya community said that they saw no viable alternative among opposition leaders, while another said that non-Yadav OBCs “have no option but to support the BJP,” because Yadavs tended to dominate the government machinery whenever the Samajwadi Party was in power. Chandra Bhushan, a professor of history at Gorakhpur University at the time, had a different take—albeit one that is fairly common in election analysis. Only Kurmis and Mauryas had the political heft to take on Yadavs, he said, while Nishads and Rajbhars were getting there. “The rest of these castes are still mostly illiterate and very much within the Hindutva fold,” Bhushan added. “For them, voting for the BJP is like voting for Hinduism.”

If anything, the truth points in the opposite direction. The upper castes have long formed a traditional and relatively stable support base for the BJP and its politics of Hindutva, and continue to do so. The EBCs’ movement towards the party has been much more recent, yet their support for the BJP is so easily labelled communal whereas upper castes are seen to be making a political choice. Why are Brahmins, Thakurs and Banias not dismissed as communal groups, given their long record of voting for the BJP? If EBCs distance themselves from the party, does that then make these communities “secular”?

Political commentary often describes EBCs who back the BJP as “silent voters” or “foot soldiers” of the party. Such language can present these communities as an instrument of someone else’s politics rather than as an autonomous political force. If a community is making a place for itself in a power structure, it is not enough to view its members simply as illiterate people who have been misled or used—we must ask whether the group itself is making political choices and what it expects in return. Similarly, instead of identifying political parties with a single caste or community, or using a negative term such as “vote cutter,” it is necessary to see which social groups it represents and what its role in participation, partnership and power distribution has been. EBCs might support the BJP today, but the party did not create the discontent that brought them there. It moved into a space left open by political parties that had failed to give many EBC communities a real share in power, and their support is something that the BJP has to continuously hold together.

title: Testimonies of police violence at the anti-SIR protests
image_caption: The Delhi Police bundle protesters into a bus during a protest on 3 October.SHAHID TANTRAY FOR THE CARAVAN
content_html:
{ONE}

NIHAL ALAM VISITED DELHI for a holiday in early October. The 36-year-old, who runs a photocopy shop in a Bihar village, had not had the chance to explore the national capital the one other time he had come. He took in the sights at Jama Masjid and the Red Fort, and caught up with friends. On 11 October, a Sunday, he wanted to buy some gifts for his family before heading home. That afternoon, Nihal stepped out with a friend—a 25-year-old Delhi resident who did not want us to name him. They went to Janpath and Palika Bazar, popular markets in the heart of Delhi, where Nihal bought some clothes and hair clips for his wife and niece.

As Nihal and his friend walked towards the Rajiv Chowk Metro Station, they saw pitched confrontations between security forces and protesters. The previous day, after the pressure group Cockroach Janta Party and several students’ organisations called for protests at Jantar Mantar to demand the resignation of the chief election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, the union government had deployed over thirty thousand police and paramilitary personnel, who prevented protesters from getting anywhere near the site. Security forces and police reportedly detained around seven thousand people, including leaders from the CJP and the student organisations. Smaller protests had continued at Connaught Place on 11 October, with security forces shutting each of them down soon after they started. Worried about the commotion, Nihal and his friend asked a nearby policeman for advice. The friend recalled that the official told them to “go bindaas”—without any worry. “Just don’t chant slogans or get caught up in the crowd.”

Minutes later, a police posse dispersing protesters charged at the pair, hitting them with lathis. Nihal’s friend was wearing clothes that made it evident that he was Muslim. Nihal recalled the policemen telling his friend, “Aren’t you ashamed roaming around like this in your beard and kurta–pyjama?” Nihal tried explaining that they were there to shop, holding up his bags as proof, and told the police that he could feel pain shooting up his arm from the blows. “These are all excuses,” he recalled one official saying. “Don’t do drama.”

title: The legends that formed around Jagdish Mahto
content_html:
“MASTER SAAB learned nothing from the outside world. Everything he knew, he taught himself.” This is a line from Mahasweta Devi’s novella Master Saab, in which a mother narrates the story of the eponymous hero to her son. The maxim is meant to kindle intrigue: why does she say that Master Saab did not learn from the outside world? What did he learn by himself? And who were his students?

First published in a Bangla literary journal in 1979, Master Saab is an intricate, embedded novella. The mother’s tale is framed by a prologue introducing the narrative time and place: Bhojpur in the early 1970s. It recounts the story of Jagdish Mahto, a renowned teacher and revolutionary from the village of Ekwari.

The novella belongs firmly to Mahasweta’s writings of the restless 1970s. Unlike the urban setting of Mother of 1084, published in 1974, or the mythic canvas of Operation? Bashai Tudu, published in 1978—her well-known novels that explore Naxalism—Master Saab is set in the fertile flatlands along the Sone Canal. Well after Independence, Bhojpur’s agrarian social order was characterised by its oppressive, casteist landed gentry and the exploitation of the Dalit peasantry. The mother’s story narrates the people’s revolt, led by Mahto, for rights and dignity against this violent feudal system. She weaves together his life’s trajectory and the long durée of Bhojpur’s militant past, stretching back to the 1930s and further back to Kunwar Singh’s exploits during the 1857 War of Independence. A fascinating literary exploration in which oral tropes blend with contemporary history, Master Saab is a tribute to collective memory and the people who created and continued the legend of the teacher.

Thirty years ago, when Mahasweta received the Jnanpith Award, the Bharatiya Jnanpith proposed a translation of one of her works. She chose Master Saab. Since then, there have been several editions of Ranjit Saha’s Hindi translation, first published in 1997. And yet, despite its significance, Master Saab has never been translated into English. Even the Bangla original continues to be anthologised in Mahasweta’s collected works but is not available as an independent work. The novella has escaped critical attention, remaining, perhaps, one of Mahasweta’s least talked about literary achievements within the formidable canon that has developed around her work on gender and identity. The unevenness of its reception testifies to her changing readership as well as to how the robust Hindi translation garnered recognition and helped retain the relevance of an episode in Bhojpur’s revolutionary history.

title: Delhi Police beats and detains a Caravan journalist during CEC protests
content_html:
The Delhi Police detained and brutally beat up The Caravan’s assistant multimedia producer, Ryan Thomas, on 11 October. Ryan was covering the protests against Gyanesh Kumar and SIR, which the government has tried to quash with an unprecedented police mobilisation in the capital, with multiple trains and metros halted, and with internet shut down across central Delhi. Earlier in the day, the Supreme Court had directed that, among other things, journalists “shall not be hindered in discharge of their professional duties in any manner whatsoever.”

Around 6 pm, on Janpath Road, as the police were detaining protesters, Ryan started following and recording a video of a group of policemen taking an individual to a detention bus parked nearby. One of them, Assistant Sub-Inspector Kapil Kumar—who was, unlike the others, wearing a name tag—turned and asked Ryan, “Tum kya kar rahe ho yeh”—what are you doing? Suddenly, three cops rushed towards Ryan and began manhandling and hitting him, while dragging him to the detention bus. Ryan repeatedly told them he is a journalist, and his press card was hanging from his neck via a lanyard and visibly displayed.

Inside the bus, five police (two more had come into the bus by then) hit Ryan on the head multiple times and tried to snatch his phone. They tried to force him to delete the images he had recorded. When he refused, stating that he was willing to cooperate with them but would not give up his phone or camera, they intensified the beating. They tried to break his camera and goaded him. One of them said, “Camera se zyada deshbhakti aa raha hai logon main aajkal”—people are feeling a bit too much nationalism because of cameras these days.

A few minutes later, about two other policemen came into the bus. They began saying “Isko doosri gadi mein le chalte hain. Isko doosri jagah le ke jaenge, kyunki ye samajh nahin raha hai”—Let’s take him elsewhere, in a different vehicle, since he is not quite getting it. Kapil Kumar handed Ryan over to these policemen. As he was being taken out of the bus, Ryan asked the two officials not to hit him, since he was cooperating with them. At that point, one of them slapped him hard on the face.

Ryan was pushed into a police car where the detainee he had been trying to record was sitting, along with three other police officials. These officials asked Ryan his name. When they heard it, they slapped him. They asked him his father’s name, and again slapped him upon hearing his answer. Again, they asked him to delete footage from his phone and hand it over. When he refused, a policeman prodded him in the stomach with the butt of his gun. At one point, a policeman pointed to a scar on his own hand and tried to insist to Ryan, “You have done this.”

Finally, the vehicle arrived at the G Block of Connaught Place, where police and paramilitary personnel were shoving more protesters into detention buses. The police threatened to put Ryan in a bus but finally let him go.

Ryan reached the emergency room at Ram Manohar Lohia Hospital at 7pm, with three colleagues from The Caravan. Upon reaching, he clearly told the RML staff that the police had beat him up while he was reporting on the protests and that he wanted a medico-legal certificate. He repeated the same to the police, as a part of the MLC proceedings. The doctors examined him and ordered some tests, including a CT scan. Once the tests were done, after more than three hours, Ryan was shown the MLC. Under the heading of “Gist of incident as stated by the injured/accompanying person,” there was a sub heading of “Alleged history.” The authorities had written “injury during protest on 11 oct 26 at 6.30pm cannaught place, c /o headache.” They did not mention that the police had caused the injury. The Delhi Police detained and brutally beat up
The Caravan
’s assistant multimedia producer, Ryan Thomas, on 11 October. Ryan was covering the protests against Gyanesh Kumar and SIR, which the government has tried to quash with an unprecedented police mobilisation in the capital, with multiple trains and metros halted, and with internet shut down across central Delhi. Earlier in the day, the Supreme Court had directed that, among other things, journalists “shall not be hindered in discharge of their professional duties in any manner whatsoever.”
Around 6 pm, on Janpath Road, as the police were detaining protesters, Ryan started following and recording a video of a group of policemen taking an individual to a detention bus parked nearby. One of them, Assistant Sub-Inspector Kapil Kumar—who was, unlike the others, wearing a name tag—turned and asked Ryan, “
Tum kya kar rahe ho yeh
”—what are you doing? Suddenly, three cops rushed towards Ryan and began manhandling and hitting him, while dragging him to the detention bus. Ryan repeatedly told them he is a journalist, and his press card was hanging from his neck via a lanyard and visibly displayed.
Inside the bus, five police (two more had come into the bus by then) hit Ryan on the head multiple times and tried to snatch his phone. They tried to force him to delete the images he had recorded. When he refused, stating that he was willing to cooperate with them but would not give up his phone or camera, they intensified the beating. They tried to break his camera and goaded him. One of them said, “Camera
se zyada deshbhakti aa raha hai logon main aajkal
”—people are feeling a bit too much nationalism because of cameras these days.
A few minutes later, about two other policemen came into the bus. They began saying “
Isko doosri gadi mein le chalte hain. Isko doosri jagah le ke jaenge, kyunki ye samajh nahin raha hai
”—Let’s take him elsewhere, in a different vehicle, since he is not quite getting it. Kapil Kumar handed Ryan over to these policemen. As he was being taken out of the bus, Ryan asked the two officials not to hit him, since he was cooperating with them. At that point, one of them slapped him hard on the face.
Ryan was pushed into a police car where the detainee he had been trying to record was sitting, along with three other police officials. These officials asked Ryan his name. Ryan reached the emergency room at Ram Manohar Lohia Hospital at 7pm, with three colleagues from
The Caravan
. Upon reaching, he clearly told the RML staff that the police had beat him up while he was reporting on the protests and that he wanted a medico-legal certificate. When he, and our other staffers, insisted that this fact be mentioned in the MLC, the authorities refused and asked them to meet the medical superintendent the next day if they wished.
The Caravan
reached out to Rajeev Ranjan, the Delhi Police public-relations officer, and Sachin Sharma, the deputy commissioner of police for the New Delhi district, but did not receive a response.

title: Fisherfolk who founded the city confront a coastal highway
image_caption: Robin William, known locally as Danger Angler, lives near Bandra Fort. During the monsoon, when taking a boat out to sea is too dangerous, he fishes from the shore with a rod.
content_html:
In South Mumbai, the coastal road is no longer the site of debate. It stands on concrete legs in the water where men used to set nets. Hemant Chandu, a fisherman from Worli Koliwada, watched it arrive. A household here once earned eight to ten lakh rupees a year, he said; it now earns about half. The drying grounds have shrunk. “The shallows our community worked for generations went under the road.” Nobody told the Kolis it was coming, Chandu said. “We found out, and we sat in protest.” The chief minister came and promised compensation, he recalled. In 2023, the Brihanmumbai Municipal Corporation set aside about Rs 130 crore for the affected fisherfolk, to be paid in instalments.

The Kolis were here before anyone else. The city stands on islands that were theirs and takes its name from Mumbadevi, a goddess they carried to the shore. Worli was the latest major koliwada—hamlet of Kolis—to be affected by the road.

To its north, the villages are waiting. It is the fourth stretch of a road that runs along the western coast of the city. The first stretch, from Marine Drive to Worli—formally named the Dharmaveer Swarajya Rakshak Chhatrapati Sambhaji Maharaj Coastal Road—is operational and was built by the BMC. From there, the Rajiv Gandhi Sea Link connects Worli to Bandra and was opened in 2010. The Maharashtra State Road Development Corporation built this and motorists are charged a toll for using it. The MSRDC is also building the Swatantrya Veer Savarkar Sea Link between Bandra and Versova, and is expected to have a toll as well. From Versova, the BMC will build the new road—26.3 kilometres, more than half of it on stilts in the sea—at an estimated cost of Rs 18,263 crore drawn from the city’s revenues. In court, the BMC explained what the money buys: a two-hour drive will take eighteen minutes.

title: What Happens to a Woman's Property After Marriage?
content_html:
The plot was always supposed to be hers. Her father bought it in Udaipur in the late 90s and when he died, Shreya, then twenty-nine, inherited it in a partition deed that her brother signed without argument. It was one of those rare moments that went exactly as the law says it ought to. But, this was the last time anything went exactly as the law said it should

Shreya got married that winter. By spring, the rent from a small shop built in the plot was being paid into an account that she did not hold. By March, the building plan had been approved on a letter signed by her husband, and within three years, a buyer made an offer, and she was told that it would be better if the whole family sat together to discuss it.

She was never told it wasn’t going to be hers, no one said that. They only ask who is going to manage it. Once a daughter’s inheritance crosses the threshold of her marital home, who actually owns it, and who actually controls it?

Like many things in the Indian family, inherited property does not have a linear journey after a woman marries. There are five checkpoints, and ownership and control can come apart at each point.

The Paper Trail
Under Section 14 of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, property a Hindu woman possesses is her absolute property. It does not become joint property with her husband if she gets married, and it does not become the property of her in-laws. And, the Supreme Court has repeated this in unusually plain language. In Maya Gopinathan v. Anoop S.B. (April, 2024), the Supreme Court reaffirmed that a woman's stridhan is her absolute property, to dispose of at her own pleasure, and that the husband has no title or independent dominion over it as an owner.

Stridhan is a specific legal category, centered on gifts to a woman before, at and after a marriage. It is not identical to inherited property. But the principle the Court draws on, that a woman;s property is her own, is the same principle that Section 14 extends to what she inherits from her parents.

The Crises of Management
A husband will be “more familiar with these things.” A father-in-law will know the local broker. A brother-in-law can “just handle it.” A power of attorney is signed, often early, “to avoid running around.” It rarely has an end date. An authority granted for convenience can easily become a habit of control. A power of attorney does not transfer ownership. But a woman who has signed one, and who has never met her own tenant, may find that the actual distance between her and her property has become very wide.
“I signed it on a Monday in June, while I made breakfast before leaving for work”, says Kavita, a thirty-eight year old working in Education in Pune. “Eight years later I realised I did not know anything about my own tenant.”
Following the Money
Rental income from a property a woman owns is, as a general rule, income that belongs to her, and income-tax law treats it that way. That means a woman is expected to report it, and pay tax on it, in her own name. Clubbing provisions, which add one spouse’s income to the other’s, apply mainly to assets a husband has transferred to his wife, and not to property she inherited from her own parents.

In reality, things happen differently. The rent goes into a joint account, or the husband’s account, or a family account used for household costs. The tax return is filed by the husband’s accountant. If the woman has a job, her own income is declared, and the rent appears, if at all, as a line she barely sees. “My CA treated it as family income for years”, says Pooja, aged forty-one, an HR consultant in Gurgaon. “I had to ask multiple times for a statement that showed the rent from my own mother’s flat in my own name.”

Can She Sell it?
Legally, yes. A woman who owns a property absolutely can sell it without her husband’s consent. A buyer’s lawyer will want her signature, not his. Socially, the answer is more complicated, and lawyers describe this familiar scene

“A woman wants to sell, let’s say, and suddenly there's a family meeting. The husband asks her if she’s sure, the in-laws ask who will invest the money, inevitably a suggestion for saving ‘for the children’ is thrown around. No one says no, they make a thousand excuses.” Sometimes a buyer, or a bank or a registrar asks for a spouse’s no objection signature. Although the law does not require it, the woman agrees to avoid delays. Over time, the exception becomes an expectation.

There is only one place where the law itself erodes a woman’s ownership, and it only becomes visible at death. Under Section 15 of the Hindu Succession Act, if a Hindu woman dies without a will and children, property she inherited will go back to her father’s heirs, and property she inherited from her husband goes back to his. The Supreme Court has described the aim as ensuring the property “goes back to the source.”

But if she dies leaving a husband or children, everything she owns, including what she inherited from her parents passes first to her husband and children. And for self-acquired property, Section 15(1)(b) places her husband’s heirs ahead of her own parents. In November, 2025 a Supreme Court bench of Justices B.V. Nagarathna and R Mahadevan heard a challenge to that provision. The court did not rule on its validity. It instead appealed to Hindu women of all ages to make wills, and directed that where a woman’s parents or their heirs claim her property after she dies without a will, the parties must try pre-litigation mediation first.

The journey of a married woman's property reveals a distinction that Indian law has largely settled and that Indian families have largely not; ownership is a legal status, control is a daily practice. Ownership is a name on a deed. Control is who answers the tenant’s phone calls, who knows the bank password, who is asked first when an offer arrives. A woman can hold the former and have none of the latter. The two tend to separate not through force, but through care. The husband who manages the rent is, in his own mind, being helpful. The father-in-law who knows a broker is saving time. Taken in confluence, they produce an owner that is not consulted. If a daughter’s education and income can be used as a reason to withhold her share of the family’s wealth, her marriage can be used as a reason to withhold control of the share she did receive. In both cases, what looks like protection can end up becoming exclusion.

title: Senior Citizen FD Rates Explained: Using an FD Calculator to Plan Your Retirement Returns
content_html:
Following retirement, while there may be fewer income sources, expenses related to household and healthcare may continue. Fixed income through interest earnings may become an integral component of the financial planning process. Knowing about senior citizen FD rates will enable them to calculate what kind of returns their savings can fetch.

For this purpose, the use of an FD calculator becomes helpful. The FD calculator takes into account the amount of deposit, the interest rate on it, the tenure, and payout frequency to estimate the interest income that can be earned.

What are senior citizen FD rates?

Senior Citizen FD interest rate refers to the interest rate for eligible investors who are 60 years old and above. Financial institutions typically offer them additional interest rate benefits above the applicable rate for customers below 60 years, depending on the product terms.

The additional interest rate can help retirees increase either their periodic income or maturity value. Nevertheless, it is important to note that the rate will differ depending on the period, deposit size, and type of payout. Investors should confirm the rate that applies to their tenure and deposit amount rather than going for the maximum rate.

Currently, Bajaj Finance Fixed Deposit provides its senior citizens with an additional interest rate benefit of up to 0.40% p.a. On a minimum investment of Rs. 15,000 to Rs. 3 crore, the annualised interest rate will be as follows starting from 7 October 2026:

How do rates affect retirement returns?

The interest rate determines how much income or maturity will be earned from the fixed deposit. The bigger the interest rate that applies to the principal and period, will earn more income.

It will be more apparent when the deposit amount or the tenure is bigger, since even the slightest change in the interest rate will have an effect on the income after a few years. It is for this reason that senior citizen FD rates should be compared on the same tenure and payment period.

The tenure that has a higher interest might indicate that the amount of money has been invested for a longer period. But it must be remembered that the retirement plan of the individual will dictate the maturity period chosen.

How does an FD calculator support retirement planning?

An FD calculator converts interest rates into estimated rupee earnings. Instead of comparing percentages alone, retirees can see the likely periodic payout or maturity amount for the sum they plan to invest.

The calculator can help answer practical questions such as:

-How much interest can a deposit generate?

-Which tenure matches a planned expense?

-What monthly income may be available?

-How does a higher rate affect returns?

-What amount may be received at maturity?

The calculations can be repeated with different amounts, rates, and tenures. This allows retirees to adjust their investment plan without completing an application or moving any money.

The displayed result remains an estimate. Tax, premature withdrawal, and changes made during booking can affect the final amount received.

Choosing between cumulative and periodic returns

In the case of cumulative Fixed Deposits, the interest remains invested in the savings account. The accrued interest generates additional interest due to compounding, and both the principal amount as well as the income are paid together.

The choice of such an account can suit retired people who have sufficient monthly income and require funds for the future. The purpose can be anything from home maintenance to healthcare to family obligations.

With regard to non-cumulative Fixed Deposits, the payment of interest can be on the basis of a certain frequency. The frequencies can range from monthly, quarterly, half-yearly, and annually.

The payout rate may differ from the rate offered at maturity. Retirees should enter the correct payout frequency in the FD calculator to obtain a relevant estimate.

Steps to calculate retirement returns

Using the calculator requires only a few basic details. Here is how retirees can compare potential returns:

1.Enter the Deposit Amount: Add the sum available for investment.

2.Select Senior Citizen: Choose the correct customer category to apply the eligible rate.

3.Choose the Tenure: Select a period aligned with the expected need for funds.

4.Pick the Payout Option: Compare interest at maturity with periodic payouts.

5.Review the Estimate: Check the interest income and maturity amount.

6.Try Other Combinations: Change the amount or tenure to compare the results.

The chosen deposit should leave enough accessible money for healthcare, household bills, and unexpected expenses. Investing every available rupee may increase dependence on premature withdrawal.

Check tax, withdrawal rules, and safety

Tax on the Interest from Fixed Deposit will be normally charged in accordance with the tax laws of the country of the investor. Tax can also be withheld at source under the prescribed conditions. Retired investors have to take into account the net rate of return after taxes while considering the expected earnings.

Withdrawal of money before maturity could lead to earning lower interest. It would be wise for investors to analyse the conditions before opening an account and keep aside some money in case of emergency.

Credit Rating needs to be considered as well. Bajaj Finance Fixed Deposit enjoys CRISIL AAA/STABLE and [ICRA] AAA(Stable) rating.

Conclusion

Comparison of retired senior citizen FD rates can assist retired people to understand the impact of their deposited money, duration of deposits, and payment frequency on their retirement income. The higher rate will not necessarily work out according to the maturity period needed by them.

The use of an FD calculator would simplify this process and would allow the calculation of approximate returns in the form of Indian Rupees. Before investing, one should consider the current interest rate, taxation, withdrawal policies, credit rating, and availability.

title: The New Indian Daughter: Will Educated Women Claim Their Inheritance?
The Wealth Gap Inside India's Middle Class
